items.claim: A frame-ancestors directive that appears in a meta element rather than a response header is not a defence, because the directive must be ignored in a policy defined via meta, so a scanner that parses the HTML and finds it has found nothing enforced.
items.disproof: It IS enforced when the same directive is also present in a real Content-Security-Policy response header, which takes precedence; it is NOT enforced when the meta-tag form is the only place it appears, in which case the page remains framable from any origin and the finding stands. The related server-side gap is that a protection header added only on success responses is missing from error and redirect responses.

How to apply it in the field: treat this as the fp_rule it is — a hunter must be able to state the concrete observation that demonstrates it, with a request and response in hand, before the finding is reportable. Boundary of the rule: It IS enforced when the same directive is also present in a real Content-Security-Policy response header, which takes precedence; it is NOT enforced when the meta-tag form is the only place it appears, in which case the page remains framable from any origin and the finding stands. items.claim: A Content-Security-Policy that defines default-src 'none' but omits frame-ancestors does not prevent framing, because frame-ancestors does not fall back to the default sources, so a hunter cannot treat a strict-looking policy as clickjacking protection.
items.disproof: It IS protection when frame-ancestors or an equivalent X-Frame-Options value is actually present and non-permissive; it is NOT when the policy relies on default-src or frame-src alone, since the spec states explicitly that an absent frame-ancestors leaves the resource framable from anywhere.

sources.quote: frame-ancestors does not fall back to the default sources when the directive is not defined.
Click-jacking protection - sets the X-Frame-Options header to control whether the page can be rendered in a frame, iframe, or object, preventing click-jacking attacks.

Boundary of the rule: It IS protection when frame-ancestors or an equivalent X-Frame-Options value is actually present and non-permissive; it is NOT when the policy relies on default-src or frame-src alone, since the spec states explicitly that an absent frame-ancestors leaves the resource framable from anywhere.

items.claim: The convincing clickjacking evidence is a PoC page that frames the target in an attacker-controlled document and demonstrates that a user interaction intended for the attacker's content lands on the framed target, which proves the UI is being redressed rather than merely that a header is absent.
items.disproof: If the framed resource refuses to load in the nested context because the ancestor check aborts the load, or the target requires a fresh interaction the attacker cannot borrow, the redressing claim collapses and only a missing-header hardening note remains; a bare 200 response to a HEAD or OPTIONS probe proves nothing about framing.

items.claim: X-Frame-Options SAMEORIGIN is defeated by an intermediate same-origin frame nested inside an attacker page, because it matches only the top-level document's location, whereas a per-ancestor check inspects every ancestor in the chain.
items.disproof: It is not defeated when the top-level document itself is the attacker origin, because the match then fails at the first ancestor; it IS defeated when the target can be embedded by one of its own pages that in turn can be framed cross-origin, since every-ancestor checking is what closes that gap.

sources.quote: many user agents implement SAMEORIGIN such that it only matches against the top-level document’s location. This directive checks each ancestor.
The ngx_http_headers_module module allows adding the “Expires” and “Cache-Control” header fields, and arbitrary fields, to a response header.

items.claim: An embeddable page is only a reportable clickjacking finding when the framed page exposes a state-changing or authenticating interaction an attacker would want to borrow; a framed page with no actionable controls is at most a low-severity hardening note.
items.disproof: It IS reportable when the framed page renders a delete, transfer, approval, or settings control reachable by the forced click; it is NOT when the framed resource is a public read-only view with no interactive elements, since nothing of value can be redressed and the missing control header carries no exploitation path.
